title: The yogis' seat
hook: tradition says the Gorakhnath yogis' center later took Nanak's name, Nanakmata

segments.voice: Yesterday, the bitter fruit made sweet, and your line, bitter made sweet. What did you take one thankful bite of? Day seven hundred thirty-four.

A campsite sign: leave it better than you found it. A rental flat with a note on the fridge from the last guests, thanking whoever comes next. Some places even take the name of a visitor who changed them. That's today's sakhi. The road has carried Guru Nanak and Mardana through oil and enchantment and bitter fruit. Now it brings them to a seat that belonged to someone else, a center of yogis, and a place that would one day carry a new name. Today: the yogis' seat.
screen: `LEAVE IT BETTER THAN YOU FOUND IT.` → `A PLACE TAKES A VISITOR'S NAME.` → `A SEAT THAT BELONGED TO OTHERS.`

segments.voice: The yogis in this story followed Gorakhnath, the teacher their order looks back to, and their center in the foothills was known by his name, Gorakhmata. We've met Gorakhnath's yogis before this year, on the mountain and at Achal, asking Nanak hard questions. Here, tradition says, the Guru comes to their own home ground and sits down under a dry, dead pipal tree. And the tree turns green. The yogis are not pleased to find a stranger on their seat. The tellings show them trying their powers to move him, and failing, and then sitting down to talk. And the talk does what talk does in these sakhis. Some of them stay to listen. In time, tradition says, the place itself took the Guru's name: Nanakmata. A gurdwara stands there now, and Sikhs go there as pilgrims. Here's what the story knows. Notice the tree. Nanak doesn't take the yogis' seat by force, and he doesn't tear anything down. The dead tree comes back to life where he sits. The tree is greener after he sits there. The story doesn't mock the yogis; Guru Nanak treated them as serious seekers, worth arguing with because they were in earnest. His hymns ask them to carry their discipline inward, to make contentment their earrings and the Name their practice. That's a visitor who leaves a place better: not by erasing what was there, but by making something grow where he sat.
screen: `GORAKHMATA, THE YOGIS' CENTER.` · `A DEAD TREE TURNS GREEN.` · `THE PLACE TAKES A NEW NAME.` · `NOT ERASED, BROUGHT BACK TO LIFE.` · then, large: `LEAVE IT BETTER.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: leave a place better. Use the sit to choose it. Settle and breathe, and look around you, or think of where you'll be in an hour. A kitchen. A desk. A bus seat. A park bench. A shared bathroom. Pick one place and one small thing: a wiped counter, a picked-up wrapper, a chair pushed in, a note of thanks. Something the next person will find without knowing who did it. If you pray, you can say Waheguru as you picture it done. The bell holds the time.
The yogis' seat. Gorakhmata, the yogis' center where tradition says a dead tree turned green under Nanak, and which came to be called Nanakmata.
Your line: leave it better. Today, do that one small thing in one shared place, and walk away without signing it. Day seven hundred thirty-four.

howItsDone: Sikhs visit Gurdwara Nanakmata Sahib as a place of pilgrimage and tell the sakhi of the yogis' seat and the pipal tree that turned green.

original.note: Punjabi, in Gurmukhi: Nanakmata, the name tradition says the yogis' center came to carry.

trapdoor: what you thought: the Guru won a contest and took over a building.
what it means: a dead tree turns green where he sits, and the place comes to carry his name.
what a scholar hears: Guru Nanak's hymns to the yogis ask them to turn outward signs inward, like contentment for earrings, so the sakhi is renewal, not erasure.

sources.ref: Janamsakhi and later Sikh tradition: Nanak at Gorakhmata (Nanakmata)
Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 6 (Japji, pauri 28: contentment as earrings)

notes: Nanakmata is in present-day Udham Singh Nagar district, Uttarakhand; left unnamed. Some histories connect the renaming with Guru Hargobind's later visit rather than Guru Nanak's; the script says only 'in time, tradition says'. Confirm.
The pipal tree turning green is from Sikh tradition about Nanakmata; confirm source (janamsakhi vs later).
Japji pauri 28 (mundaa santokh: contentment as earrings) paraphrased; confirm Ang 6.
Earlier y3 days (Mount Sumer, Achal) referenced as 'on the mountain and at Achal'; confirm those days covered Gorakhnath's yogis.
Editor: cut the glosses 'the seat of Gorakh' and 'the seat of Nanak' (an etymology no cited text gives) from voice, screen, match and original note; cut 'places remember how we treated them'.

Auditor: 'whatever the place had been ... bringing it back to life' read as framing the yogis' center as dead or lesser; reworded so only the tree is renewed and Gorakhnathi tradition is not the foil.
